description: Realtors can work fewer hours by batching admin, checking email in set windows, and using Gmail templates. Free Mac and Gmail fixes, plus Lazur help.

intro: Realtors can work fewer hours by giving non-selling work a fixed place in the week. Stop answering email all day, turn repeat replies into templates, and batch the rest into set blocks. The typical Realtor works a median of 35 hours a week, so small changes to admin time add up.
tldr: Give admin fixed blocks in your day instead of answering it all day.
One study of 124 adults found people felt less stressed when they checked email less often.
Gmail templates and scheduled sends remove repeat typing from your week.
Measure your own week first. No source I could open measures how much of it is admin.

blocks.text: Why a normal week runs long

The National Association of Realtors reported in its 2026 Member Profile, using 2025 data, that the typical Realtor works a median of 35 hours a week. That figure did not change from the year before. Sales agents median 30 hours a week. Brokers and managers who also sell median 40 to 45 hours. A median means half of agents work more than that, so the number is a baseline, not a ceiling.

A median hour count does not show how those hours split. Selling work includes showings, prospecting conversations, negotiating, and writing offers. Non-selling work includes chasing signatures, answering the same question again, updating a tracker, and rewriting listing copy. I could not find a primary study that measures how much of a Realtor's week goes to that second list. Vendor blogs quote admin shares. Treat those as marketing until you see the data behind them.
Track your own week before you change anything

Start with a plain log. For one working week, write down each non-selling task as you finish it. Keep the log in a note on your Mac or on paper. Put a mark beside every line that does not move a deal forward. Write what you did, not what you planned to do.

At the end of the week, read the marked lines and look for repeats. If you answered the same question about parking, pets, or HOA dues again and again, that question needs a template. If you rebuilt the same status update in several places, that update needs one tracker. The log tells you where to start, which beats a list of generic tips.
The log also shows when you work. Note the time each task started. If most non-selling work starts after dinner, the problem is not your daytime schedule. It is the habit of answering from the couch.
What non-selling work costs you

Time is the obvious cost, but it is not the only one. Admin pushed into evenings and weekends eats rest. The Bureau of Labor Statistics says real estate schedules often include evenings and weekends, and most brokers and sales agents work full time. When the day already runs long, admin takes the hours meant for recovery.

Slow replies can cost you deals. Harvard Business Review published The Short Life of Online Sales Leads in 2011. The article opens with the finding that most companies are not responding nearly fast enough to sales leads. It covers companies in general, not real estate agents. Still, a buyer who fills out a form and hears nothing may call someone else.

Constant checking also costs you focus and mood. In a study by Kushlev and Dunn, 124 adults were split into two groups. Some were asked to limit email checks to three times a day for a week. Others could check as often as they liked. Across the study, people felt less stressed when they checked email less often. The study measured stress, not sales or hours.
Why it keeps happening

Most agents work for themselves. BLS reports that 54% of sales agents are self-employed. That means nobody else owns the admin. No office manager sends the reminder. No employer covers the hour you spend on it. If you do not decide where admin goes, it fills whatever space is open.

Your phone makes that space endless. NAR's 2026 Member Profile says 96% of Realtors use a smartphone daily or nearly every day for business. It also says 93% use email daily or nearly daily. Your inbox comes with you to showings, closings, and dinner. Each buzz asks for a small decision, and small decisions pile up faster than you expect.
Email windows instead of constant checks

The fix most people skip is the simplest one. Choose a few email times that fit your work, such as first thing in the morning, midday, and before you log off. Check mail only in those windows, unless a client needs a same-day answer. Tell clients which hours you reply, so they know what to expect.

Make the windows real by quieting the noise. Open Apple menu > System Settings > Notifications. If Google Chrome appears in that list, turn off its banners. Keep phone calls on. A missed call and a missed email carry different costs, and a seller who calls needs a route to you.

Test the windows for one week. If a buyer or seller truly needed you in between, write that down. One real exception is useful information. A long list of exceptions means your windows are too tight, so move them rather than giving up on them.
Gmail templates for the replies you send every week

A template saves you from retyping the same answer. In Gmail on your Mac, click the gear icon, then See all settings. Open the Advanced tab, find Templates, choose Enable, and click Save Changes at the bottom of the page.

To save a template, write a reply once in a new message. Then click the three-dot More options icon at the bottom of the compose window. Choose Templates, then Save draft as template. Name it so you can find it fast, such as Showing thanks or Document request.

Good first templates are the replies you send most. Showing confirmations, document requests, the answer to the same HOA question, and the follow up after a showing are strong starts. Use placeholders such as [Property address] and read each one before you send. A template with the wrong street name is worse than a slow reply. For real estate specific setup, see [Gmail for realtors on Mac](/for/realtors/gmail).
Scheduled sends for late-night writing

If you write at night, schedule the send for morning. Click the arrow beside Send, choose Schedule send, and pick a time. Scheduling lets you finish the message when you have the thought, and it goes out at a sensible hour.

Do not schedule a reply you cannot stand behind. If a buyer answers early, a scheduled reply that ignores the new facts makes you look careless. Open the Scheduled folder before the send time, and edit or delete the message if the situation changed.
Filters keep low-urgency mail out of your way

Gmail filters handle mail that never needs a fast answer. Click the gear icon, choose See all settings, then open Filters and Blocked Addresses. Click Create a new filter, enter the sender or words, and choose Create filter. Pick Skip the Inbox, then apply a label so the mail waits in one place.

Use filters for newsletters, portal digests, vendor receipts, and marketing from title companies. Do not filter buyers, sellers, or lenders into a folder you check once a week. Those messages need a route that reaches you in your morning window.
A tracker in Google Sheets, not in your head

Much admin is status tracking. Which listing needs a disclosure? Which buyer waits on a lender? Put one deal per row in a Google Sheets file. Add a Status column, select it, and choose Data > Data validation. Set the criteria to a dropdown list of statuses, so each status is picked, not typed.

A plain tracker still needs upkeep, so keep updates short. Put the next action in one column and its due date in another. One short update in the same place beats long notes spread across apps. For commission math and deal tracker setup, see [Google Sheets for realtors on Mac](/for/realtors/google-sheets).

blocks.text: Put admin on a schedule with Shortcuts

The Shortcuts app is built into your Mac, so it adds no cost. Apple's guide says you add an automation by clicking Edit, then Automation, then choosing a trigger. Time of Day is one trigger. Pick the time, add an action that opens the pages you need, and the automation runs on your schedule.

Apple's guide says some personal automations can run without confirmation. It also says an automation set this way does not notify you when it triggers. Read that before you turn it on. Start with one shortcut that opens your Gmail and tracker at the start of your admin window.
Mistakes that make the problem worse

items: Building a full template library in one afternoon. Start with the replies you send most, then add more only when you repeat a new one.
Silencing everything, including calls from buyers, sellers, and lenders. A few channels should always reach you.
Filtering clients into a folder you check once a week, which hides urgent work from you.
Scheduling sends and never reading the replies that come back.
Building a tracker with every detail. Keep only the fields you use to decide the next step.
Pasting client personal information into any tool before you check your brokerage's rules.

blocks.text: Client data, brokerage rules, and AI tools

Realtors handle personal and financial details, so check your brokerage's rules before you use any AI tool with client files. Some offices have written policies on what you may paste, dictate, or screenshot. Follow those rules even when a tool seems harmless. When in doubt, keep client identifiers out of the text.

Do not dictate Social Security numbers, bank account details, or full loan documents. Lazur listens and looks only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer your question, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.
What Lazur does, and where it stops

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a setting is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. You stay in control of Gmail, Sheets, and the Shortcuts app. For this problem, Lazur is most useful for small jobs. It can draft a reply, dictate a note, set a timer, or explain a setting you keep forgetting.

Dictation works in any app. Hold fn and speak, and Lazur types clean, formatted text at your cursor. It also keeps snippets, a personal dictionary, and clipboard slots. Use a snippet for the paragraph you paste into every listing follow up. Dictation is unlimited on both paid plans, but it is not the main reason to choose Lazur.

Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension. It comes back with a summary and a report. Use it to read background sources, then open the originals yourself before you rely on them.

Lazur has a free Pro trial that starts when you first open the app, and no credit card is needed. Current plan prices are on the [pricing page](/pricing). Compare those prices with the hours you expect to save, not with a promise of what the tool will do.
A worked example for one busy week

Take a busy week with showings on Monday. Under the old routine, you answer email between showings on your phone. Then you finish the same replies after dinner. Under the new routine, you check mail in your set windows. Replies you send often come from templates. Anything that needs judgment waits for the next window.

On Thursday, a buyer's agent emails a question late in the evening. Under the old routine, you would answer from bed. Under the new one, you draft a reply from a template or by dictation, then schedule the send for the morning window. Check the tracker first, so the reply matches the deal's status.

On Friday, read your log and compare it with the Monday entries. If the non-selling column barely moved, look at what repeats. Each repeat becomes the next template, filter, or tracker column. Keep the routine for a few weeks before you change it again.
Edge cases that change the fix

Some offices hand admin to a transaction coordinator. If yours does, your fix starts with the handoff. Write a short checklist of what goes to them and what you still own. Do not assume they will catch a missing signature on your deal.

Templates depend on language your brokerage approves. Some disclosures and contract wording must come from the brokerage or the form itself, so do not rewrite them in your own words. Use templates for the friendly parts, and check any legal text against your brokerage's standard.

If your email windows keep breaking, look at your deal pipeline before you blame your discipline. A busy month with many closings pushes admin into every window. Protect one window that nothing else can take, and let the rest flex.
What to do next

Start with the email windows today. It costs nothing, and it shows you how much of your day is reactive. Build one template and one filter this week. Add the tracker once you know which status columns you actually use. If you want help with each setting, [download Lazur](/download) and ask it to walk you through one click at a time.

faq.question: How many hours do Realtors work per week?
faq.answer: NAR's 2026 Member Profile, covering 2025, puts the typical Realtor at a median of 35 hours a week. Sales agents median 30 hours, and brokers who also sell median 40 to 45 hours. Medians hide a lot, so track your own week before you compare yourself with anyone.

faq.question: Can I work fewer hours and keep my business running?
faq.answer: Often, yes, if the time you cut is admin and not showings or prospecting. Measure first. Then cut repeat work and protect selling time with fixed blocks. No source I could open shows how much admin time can be cut, so test the change for a few weeks.

faq.question: Does checking email less really help?
faq.answer: A study by Kushlev and Dunn with 124 adults found people felt less stressed when they checked email less often. The study measured stress, not hours or sales, and it did not test Realtors. It is a reason to try windows, not proof they will save you time.

faq.question: Is it safe to use AI tools with client information?
faq.answer: Follow your brokerage's written rules first. Lazur listens and looks only while you hold the shortcut, and audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer you without being stored. Do not dictate Social Security numbers, bank details, or full loan documents.

faq.question: Do I need Lazur to fix this problem?
faq.answer: No. Gmail templates, scheduled sends, filters, Google Sheets dropdowns, and the Shortcuts app cost nothing extra. Lazur helps with drafting, dictation, explaining settings, and answering questions out loud while you work.

faq.question: Will Lazur click the buttons for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It points at things on screen, guides you one click at a time, drafts text, dictates into the cursor, and answers out loud.

costs.title: Evenings and weekends
costs.text: Real estate schedules often include evenings and weekends, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Admin that spills past dinner takes the hours you need to rest. The next day starts tired, and slow admin gets slower.

costs.title: Slower replies to leads
costs.text: A Harvard Business Review article on online sales leads opens by saying most companies are not responding nearly fast enough. A buyer who hears nothing may call someone else. Batching admin should never leave a fresh inquiry waiting until the end of the day.

costs.title: Constant interruptions
costs.text: In the Kushlev and Dunn study, people felt less stressed when they checked email less often. Every check is a small interruption. Less stress is a cost you feel every day, even though it never appears on a timesheet.

costs.title: Hours that do not close deals
costs.text: NAR's data puts the typical Realtor at a median of 35 hours a week. Hours spent on admin are hours not spent on showings, prospecting, or negotiating. No client pays for most of that admin directly, so the real cost is lost selling time.

causes.title: Nobody else owns the admin
causes.text: Most brokers and sales agents are self-employed, and BLS reports that 54% of sales agents fall in that group. Without an office manager or employer, the admin lands on you by default. It shows up as an open loop that nobody else will close.

causes.title: Your inbox travels with you
causes.text: NAR's 2026 Member Profile says 96% of Realtors use a smartphone daily or nearly every day for business, and 93% use email that often. Constant access means every message asks for a fresh decision. Those decisions use up the day before you notice.

causes.title: Replies feel urgent by default
causes.text: Lead speed matters, and the Harvard Business Review article on sales leads makes that case. Many agents treat every message as urgent. Without a rule for what counts as urgent, the inbox sets your priorities for you.

causes.title: Repeat work has no template
causes.text: The same questions about parking, pets, HOA dues, and inspection dates arrive again and again. Each one gets typed from scratch. Repeated answers are the easiest admin to remove, and they are often the first thing to wear you down.

causes.title: Status lives in your head
causes.text: When deal status lives in memory, you answer the same status questions by phone. Each call is an interruption and a piece of admin at once. One tracker with a status column turns those calls into a quick look.

fixes.title: Set email windows
fixes.text: Choose a few fixed times to check email, such as first thing, midday, and before you log off. Outside those times, keep the inbox closed unless a client needs a same-day answer. The Kushlev and Dunn study links less checking to less stress. Tell clients your reply hours so they expect them.

fixes.title: Turn repeat replies into templates
fixes.text: Write the replies you send most, then save each one as a Gmail template with Save draft as template. Start with showing confirmations, document requests, and HOA questions. Gmail templates cost nothing extra. Check every placeholder before you send.

fixes.title: Filter low-urgency mail
fixes.text: Create a Gmail filter for newsletters, portal digests, and vendor receipts. Apply a label and choose Skip the Inbox. Keep buyers, sellers, and lenders out of filters so their mail still reaches your morning window.

fixes.title: Keep one deal tracker
fixes.text: Use one Google Sheets file with one row per deal. Add a Status column with a dropdown from Data > Data validation, and a Next action column with a due date. One place for status means fewer calls asking where a file stands.

fixes.title: Schedule admin with Shortcuts
fixes.text: Use the Shortcuts app on your Mac to run an automation at the start of your admin window. Apple's guide says you click Edit, then Automation, then pick a trigger such as Time of Day. Add an action that opens your inbox and tracker together.
